messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was fifty-five years old when the industrial fire at Riverside Chemical Plant consumed the warehouse where he had been conducting a routine safety consultation on a Tuesday afternoon in March. He had been a counselor for twenty-eight years—first in corporate wellness, then in trauma-informed workplace intervention—and he prided himself on his calm, measured presence in crisis situations. The fire alarm had sounded at 2:47 p.m. He remembered the time because he had glanced at his watch, thinking it was likely a drill. It was not a drill. Within minutes, the loading dock where he stood had become engulfed in thick, acrid smoke. The smell—chemical, choking, almost alive in its intensity—had filled his lungs before he could process what was happening. He had made it out, along with three others, but two workers who had been in the adjacent storage area did not. The flames had moved with terrifying speed. The smell had stayed with him longer than anything else—not just in his nostrils but embedded in his memory in a way that felt more real than the visual details of escape.

In the weeks after the fire, Marcus had returned to work, reasoning that avoidance would only compound the trauma. But something had shifted in how his body inhabited the world. The smell of burnt toast at a coffee shop would send his heart racing; the acrid scent of a neighbor's fireplace in autumn would leave him rigid and sweating for hours. Worse, sometimes he would smell smoke when there was no smoke—phantom olfactory sensations that seemed to materialize from nowhere, pulling the full weight of that afternoon's terror into his chest without warning or image. These moments were the most disorienting. He would feel the panic, the suffocation, the helplessness in their complete intensity, but when he tried to locate what he was remembering, there was only fog. The memory felt like it belonged to someone else, something he had watched happen to a stranger rather than lived through himself.

Around the same time, Marcus had begun to notice that his body no longer felt like his ally. His heart would race unpredictably; his breathing would become shallow and rapid in moments of ordinary stress. He had come to believe that his body was betraying him, reacting as if danger were imminent when logically he knew he was safe in his office or his apartment. This fundamental mistrust had gradually reshaped his daily life. He stopped attending the monthly counselor's peer group he had facilitated for years, telling himself that he needed time to process, but really fearing that his colleagues would notice something wrong, that his thoughts might scatter in front of them, that he might not be able to hold the container they relied on him to hold. He avoided his closest friend, David, who had called repeatedly after the fire. When David finally showed up at his door one evening, Marcus had felt a surge of panic—not at David's presence, but at the thought that David would see him struggling, would ask direct questions, would force him to articulate the thoughts that now occupied his mind constantly.

Because Marcus had become hypervigilant in a way that felt necessary. He monitored his own thinking with exhausting precision, watching for signs that he was losing coherence, that the trauma was fracturing him beyond repair. If he allowed himself to think about the fire—really think about it—he was certain he would not be able to handle the weight of it. So he had constructed an elaborate internal barrier against reflection. He did not watch the news. He did not read the follow-up articles about the investigation. When his mind drifted toward the memory, he would redirect it forcefully, sometimes by leaving whatever room he was in, sometimes by engaging in repetitive tasks. The avoidance had become its own exhausting work.

Now, six months after the fire, Marcus sat in his own office—the place where he had spent nearly three decades helping others navigate their psychological crises—and realized he could no longer manage alone. His professional reputation remained intact, but his internal world had become a place of constant vigilance and fear. He had begun to wonder if the person who had walked out of that burning warehouse was actually still here at all, or if something essential had been left behind in the smoke. What brought him finally to seek help was not a dramatic crisis but a quiet recognition: he had become a stranger to himself, and he did not know how to find his way back.
